title: Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2026

Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2026

# Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report

## Jobs at the Center of Poverty Eradication

Global progress on reducing extreme poverty has come to a standstill, and the world is at risk of falling further behind, according to the new Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026: Jobs at the Center of Poverty Eradication. Without stronger per capita growth, the number of people in extreme poverty is projected to be higher in 2030 than it is today. The report finds that creating more and better jobs is a powerful lever to lift people out of poverty.

Download, explore and share the findings from the Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026: Jobs at the Center of Poverty Eradication. 

## Extreme poverty reduction has stalled and might rise

In 2026, 811 million people, 1 in 10, live on less than $3.00 a day, a rate unchanged since 2019. More than half the extreme poor live in nine economies, and by 2030, 87 percent will be in Sub-Saharan Africa, in fragile and conflict-affected situations, or both. Without stronger per capita growth, the number of people in extreme poverty is projected to be higher in 2030 than it is today.

Despite the reduction seen in past decades, escaping extreme poverty has not meant reaching security. Nearly half of humanity, 3.7 billion people, still lives on less than $8.30 a day, most of them one shock away from falling back.

## Progress toward shared prosperity has slowed

The Prosperity Gap, which captures how far the world is from a dignified and secure daily standard of living, halved between 1990 and 2013, but it has narrowed by barely 1 percent a year since. One in five people worldwide, and more than a third of the people living in extreme poverty, lives in an economy with high levels of inequality.

## Climate-related shocks threaten the progress against poverty 

Of the 4.6 billion people living in areas exposed to major climate-related hazards, 1.5 billion are in a highly vulnerable situation because they lack social protection or access to basic infrastructure. While the high-risk share declined from 1 in 3 people in 2010 to 1 in 6 people in 2024, the number of people exposed rose by about 550 million.

Climate risk is widespread and emissions are rising where the poor are not

#### Ending extreme poverty would barely add to global emissions

The effort to eradicate extreme poverty is estimated to add less than 5 percent to global emissions. The extreme poor contribute the least to global emissions but are the most vulnerable to the consequences of climate change. 

## More jobs and better-paid jobs are needed to reduce poverty 

Nearly all poor households hold a single productive asset: human capital. This makes employment — quantity and quality — the central lever for poverty reduction.

Closing employment gaps in poor households to a benchmark of 75% of working-age adults would reduce extreme poverty by a fifth, with the gain going mainly to workers above the extreme poverty line — where the nonworking adults are mostly women.

Raising the earnings of poor workers toward what comparable nonpoor workers earn could cut poverty by nearly half, with the gain going mainly to the poorest households.

Change in the probability of escaping poverty from a move into wage employment, by income group

 Source: Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026: Jobs at the Center of Poverty Eradication. World Bank Group. 

 Note: The figure illustrates the change in the probability of escaping poverty (percentage points). Bars: ordinary least square coefficients (×10) from linear probability models of exiting poverty (poor at baseline, nonpoor at endline) on the change in the household share of working-age members (ages 15–64) in wage employment and in nonwage employment (self-employment in agriculture, self-employment in nonagriculture, and employer, consolidated into one variable). Poverty status is measured against the income-group–specific international poverty line (2021 purchasing power parity). Whiskers are 95 percent confidence intervals. Sample: initially poor households. 

## Key Messages at a Glance

 1. Poverty reduction has stalled. 

In 2026, 811 million people, 1 in 10, are living on less than $3.00 a day, a rate unchanged since 2019. Had the pace of 2000–13 continued, 243 million fewer people would be poor today.

 2. Extreme poverty is becoming concentrated, and the rate will rise. 

More than half of the extreme poor are living in nine economies, and, by 2030, 87 percent will be in Sub-Saharan Africa, in fragile and conflict-affected situations, or both. At the growth rates of the past decade, both the global rate and the number of the extreme poor will be higher in 2030 than today.

 3. Escaping extreme poverty has not meant reaching security. 

Nearly half of humanity, 3.7 billion people, are still living on less than $8.30 a day. Most of these people are one shock away from falling back into poverty.

 4. Progress toward shared prosperity has slowed. 

The Prosperity Gap, which captures how far the world is from a dignified and secure daily standard of living, was reduced by half between 1990 and 2013, but it has narrowed by barely 1 percent a year since then. One in five people worldwide and more than a third of the extreme poor are living in high-inequality economies.

 5. Ending extreme poverty would scarcely add to emissions. 

The growth needed to end extreme poverty would add less than 5 percent to global emissions.

 6. Climate-related shocks threaten the progress against poverty. 

Around 1.5 billion people, most of whom are living above the extreme poverty line, are exposed to climate hazards and lack the means to cope with a shock.

 7. The poor work, but their work pays too little. 

Adults in poor households are employed at rates only 6 percentage points below the rates among the nonpoor, yet earn far less per household member, and their employment has been eroding, falling in 88 of 138 economies over 2003–24.

 8. More jobs and better-paying jobs both reduce poverty, but they reach different people. 

Closing employment gaps affecting poor households to a benchmark of 75 percent of working-age adults would reduce extreme poverty by a fifth. The gain would benefit mainly the near-poor, among whom most nonworking adults are women. Raising the earnings among poor workers to the level among comparable nonpoor workers could cut poverty by nearly half, and the gain would benefit primarily the poorest.

 9. The implication for the jobs agenda. 

In the poorest economies, the near-term gains of more jobs reside in the productivity of farms and household enterprises and in integrating women into the workforce. Meanwhile, the better-paying jobs route leads to good returns as firms grow. More and better jobs are thus both needed, but the sequencing differs.

## Resources

The Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report is the World Bank Group's flagship biennial publication tracking global progress on ending extreme poverty and boosting shared prosperity on a livable planet.
